content.glance: BNS s. 42 — When such right extends to causing any harm other than death.

sections.heading: The legal rule
sections.body: 42. If the offence, the committing of which, or the attempting to commit which occasions the exercise of the right of private defence, be theft, mischief, or criminal trespass, not of any of the descriptions specified in section 41, that right does not extend to the voluntary causing of death, but does extend, subject to the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing to the wrong-doer of any harm other than death

learningObjectives: Understand the non-lethal boundaries of property defence under BNS s. 42.
Identify the property offences where death cannot be caused.
Apply the rule of proportionality in protecting property.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 42 provides that if the offence, the committing of which, or the attempting to commit which occasions the exercise of the right of private defence, be theft, mischief, or criminal trespass, not of any of the descriptions enumerated in section 41, that right does not extend to the voluntary causing of death, but does extend, under the restrictions mentioned in section 37, to the voluntary causing to the wrong-doer of any harm other than death.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: For ordinary property offences (daytime theft, simple mischief, ordinary criminal trespass), the owner or defender is legally entitled to use necessary physical force to expel the trespasser or recover property, but cannot intentionally cause the wrong-doer's death.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 42 (corresponding to IPC s. 104).
Scope: Theft, mischief, or criminal trespass NOT covered by s. 41.
Harm limit: Prohibits voluntary causing of death.
Permitted harm: Extends to causing any harm other than death subject to s. 37.
essentialIngredients: The offence is theft, mischief, or criminal trespass.
The offence does NOT involve the grave circumstances specified in s. 41.
The defender causes non-lethal harm to prevent or terminate the crime.
The force used is proportionate under s. 37.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 42 governs ordinary daytime property disputes. If someone trespasses onto a farmer's field, tries to cut his crop, or attempts to steal cattle without weapons, the owner has every right to use physical force: pushing, grappling, brandishing a lathi, or striking non-lethal blows to drive the offender off. However, the owner cannot shoot, stab in vital organs, or beat the thief to death. If death is caused, the owner exceeds private defence and is liable for culpable homicide.
examples: Teaching example (Ejecting a trespasser): A landowner finds an unauthorized squatter pitching a tent on his private lawn. The squatter refuses to leave. The landowner uses physical force to push the squatter out and tosses the tent onto the road, causing minor bruises to the squatter. Section 42 protects the landowner.

Teaching example (Killing a fruit thief): A orchard owner spots a youth plucking mangoes from a tree at midday. The owner shoots the youth dead with a hunting rifle. Section 42 is violated; killing an unarmed thief is culpable homicide.
distinctions: Section 41 vs Section 42: Section 41 allows lethal force for 4 extreme property crimes; Section 42 allows only non-lethal force for ordinary property crimes.
Daytime trespass vs Night house-breaking: Daytime trespass falls under s. 42 (non-lethal); night house-breaking falls under s. 41 (lethal).
problemApplication: Issue: What is the liability of a shopkeeper who broke the arm of a thief attempting to run away with a display jacket?
Rule: BNS s. 42 permits voluntary causing of any harm other than death to defend property against theft.
Application: Breaking the arm was non-lethal force used in direct resistance to the theft. Death was not caused, and force was within s. 37 bounds.
Conclusion: Section 42 applies; the shopkeeper is exempt from criminal liability.
